detail:
NIH Research Matters reports on pain reprocessing therapy, a psychological treatment studied for chronic back pain that is based on retraining how the brain interprets pain signals. According to the report, the approach teaches participants that many cases of chronic back pain involve the brain generating pain in the absence of ongoing tissue damage, and that reappraising pain as non-threatening can reduce the fear and amplification that keep it going. In the randomized study described, participants receiving pain reprocessing therapy reported substantially larger pain reductions than comparison groups, and many reported being pain-free or nearly pain-free after treatment, with gains largely maintained at follow-up.

NIH presents the findings as evidence that brain-based approaches merit further study, not as a guarantee of results or a replacement for medical evaluation. Sources note that the study involved a selected group of people with primary chronic back pain, that secondary back pain from a specific structural or medical cause is a different situation requiring its own workup, and that researchers continue to study which patients benefit most and how durable the effects are.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about chronic low back pain research and treatment options.
summary: NIH Research Matters describes a randomized study of pain reprocessing therapy for primary chronic back pain, in which retraining how the brain appraises pain was linked to large, largely maintained pain reductions.
takeaways: pain reprocessing therapy targets how the brain appraises pain signals
the study reported large reductions in a selected primary pain group
sources present brain-based approaches as an area for further study
title: Chronic Low Back Pain: retraining how the brain processes pain
